<div class="accordion-item"><h2 class="accordion-header"><button class="accordion-button collapsed" type="button" data-bs-toggle="collapse" data-bs-target="#work-acc-summary">Summary</button></h2><div id="work-acc-summary" class="accordion-collapse collapse"><div class="accordion-body">Kappaṇṇābhyudaya is a Sanskrit epic poem written by the 9th-century AD poet Bhaṭṭaśivasvāmi. The poem is divided into seven chapters, each of which tells a different part of the story of Kappaṇṇa, a young Brāhmaṇa  boy who is falsely accused of stealing a precious gem.<br>The first chapter describes Kappaṇṇa's childhood and his love of learning. The second chapter tells of his marriage to a young woman named Suraṅganā, who is later accused of stealing the gem. In the third chapter, Kappaṇṇa is accused of the crime, and he and his wife are banished from their village.<br><br>In the fourth chapter, Kappaṇṇa and Suraṅganā travel to the city of Kāñcī, where Kappaṇṇa becomes a respected scholar and teacher. In the fifth chapter, Kappaṇṇa is falsely accused of stealing again and is imprisoned, but he is eventually freed by his former student.<br>In the sixth chapter, Kappaṇṇa and Suraṅganā return to their village, where they are reunited with their families. Finally, in the seventh chapter, Kappaṇṇa is vindicated when the true thief is caught and the stolen gem is returned.<br>Throughout the poem, Bhaṭṭaśivasvāmi uses elaborate metaphors and intricate wordplay to describe Kappaṇṇa's trials and tribulations. The poem is also notable for its use of complex grammatical structures, which are typical of the kāvya style of Sanskrit poetry.</div></div></div>
<div class="accordion-item"><h2 class="accordion-header"><button class="accordion-button collapsed" type="button" data-bs-toggle="collapse" data-bs-target="#work-acc-contents">Contents</button></h2><div id="work-acc-contents" class="accordion-collapse collapse"><div class="accordion-body">Kappaṇṇābhyudaya is a Sanskrit epic poem that consists of seven chapters, each of which tells a different part of the story of Kappaṇṇa, a young Brahmin boy who is falsely accused of stealing a precious gem.<br>Chapter 1: The first chapter of the poem introduces the protagonist, Kappaṇṇa, and describes his childhood and love of learning. Kappaṇṇa is depicted as a bright and curious boy who is interested in philosophy, logic, and the Vedas.<br>Chapter 2: In the second chapter, Kappaṇṇa marries Suraṅganā, a young woman who is known for her beauty and intelligence. Suraṅganā is later accused of stealing a valuable gem, and Kappaṇṇa is falsely accused of the crime.<br>Chapter 3: The third chapter describes Kappaṇṇa's trial and banishment from his village. Kappaṇṇa and Suraṅganā set out on a journey to prove their innocence and find a new home.<br>Chapter 4: In the fourth chapter, Kappaṇṇa and Suraṅganā arrive in the city of Kāñcī, where Kappaṇṇa becomes a respected scholar and teacher. The chapter also introduces a new character, a wealthy merchant named Dhanika.<br>Chapter 5: The fifth chapter tells of Kappaṇṇa's imprisonment and eventual release. Kappaṇṇa is falsely accused of stealing again, and he is thrown into prison. However, he is eventually freed by one of his former students.<br>Chapter 6: In the sixth chapter, Kappaṇṇa and Suraṅganā return to their village, where they are reunited with their families. Kappaṇṇa is invited to participate in a competition of learned men, and he wins the competition with his intellectual prowess.<br>Chapter 7: The seventh and final chapter of the poem sees Kappaṇṇa finally vindicated when the true thief is caught and the stolen gem is returned. Kappaṇṇa and Suraṅganā are welcomed back into their village with honour and respect.<br>Throughout the poem, Bhaṭṭaśivasvāmi uses elaborate metaphors, intricate wordplay, and complex grammatical structures to describe Kappaṇṇa's trials and tribulations. The poem is a masterful example of the kāvya style of Sanskrit poetry and is still studied and appreciated by scholars today.</div></div></div>
<div class="accordion-item"><h2 class="accordion-header"><button class="accordion-button collapsed" type="button" data-bs-toggle="collapse" data-bs-target="#work-acc-uniqueness">Uniqueness</button></h2><div id="work-acc-uniqueness" class="accordion-collapse collapse"><div class="accordion-body">Kappaṇṇābhyudaya is a unique work of Sanskrit poetry due to its intricate wordplay, complex grammatical structures, and extensive use of metaphors. Bhaṭṭaśivasvāmi's skilful use of language is evident throughout the poem, and it sets Kappaṇṇābhyudaya apart from other works of its time. The poem is also notable for its strong character development, particularly in its depiction of Kappaṇṇa and his wife Suraṅganā. Kappaṇṇābhyudaya is a valuable example of the kāvya style of Sanskrit poetry and continues to be studied and appreciated by scholars of Indian literature.</div></div></div>
<div class="accordion-item"><h2 class="accordion-header"><button class="accordion-button collapsed" type="button" data-bs-toggle="collapse" data-bs-target="#work-acc-contribution">Contribution &amp; Notes</button></h2><div id="work-acc-contribution" class="accordion-collapse collapse"><div class="accordion-body">Kappaṇṇābhyudaya is a significant contribution to Sanskrit literature due to its masterful use of language, intricate wordplay, and complex grammatical structures. Bhaṭṭaśivasvāmi's skilful writing and poetic prowess are evident throughout the work, making it a valuable example of the kāvya style of Sanskrit poetry. The poem's strong character development, particularly in its portrayal of Kappaṇṇa and Suraṅganā, also adds to its importance in Sanskrit literature. Kappaṇṇābhyudaya is a unique and well-crafted work that continues to be studied and appreciated by scholars of Indian literature, contributing to the rich legacy of Sanskrit poetry.<br><br>Apart from being an important literary work, Kappaṇṇābhyudaya is also a valuable source of information about the social, cultural, and political conditions of Kashmir during the 9th century. It provides insights into the life of the common people, the role of women in society, and the patronage of the ruling elite towards poets and scholars. Additionally, the work has been admired for its use of vivid descriptions, metaphors, and similes, which make it a delightful read for lovers of Sanskrit literature.</div></div></div>
